title: Canteen Bill Discount
statement:
The college canteen gives a 10% discount on any bill of Rs 500 or more. The discount is rounded down to a whole rupee (it is bill // 10). Bills below Rs 500 get no discount.

Input: one line with an integer bill (1 <= bill <= 10000).
Output: one integer, the amount to pay.

Example: for input 650 the discount is 65, so print 585.
starterCode:
bill = int(input())
# your code here

examples.explanation: 650 is at least 500, so 65 is taken off.

referenceSolution:
bill = int(input())
if bill >= 500:
    bill = bill - bill // 10
print(bill)
hints: Compare the bill with 500 using if.
The discount is bill // 10; subtract it only when the bill qualifies.
explanation: Read the bill and check whether it is at least 500. If it is, subtract bill // 10; otherwise leave it unchanged. Print the result.

title: Leap Year Check
statement:
A year is a leap year if it is divisible by 400, or if it is divisible by 4 but not by 100.

Input: one integer year (1 <= year <= 9999).
Output: print Leap if it is a leap year, otherwise print Not Leap.

Example: 2024 is divisible by 4 and not by 100, so print Leap.
starterCode:
year = int(input())
# your code here

examples.explanation: 2024 is divisible by 4 and not by 100.
1900 is divisible by 100 but not by 400.

hints: Use the % operator to test divisibility.
Check the 400 rule first, or combine the rules with and / or.
explanation: Combine the three divisibility rules into one condition: divisible by 400, or divisible by 4 and not by 100. Print Leap when it holds, Not Leap otherwise.

title: Who Won the Match
statement:
Team A and Team B played a T20 match. Given both final scores, announce the result.

Input: one line with two integers a and b separated by a space (0 <= a, b <= 500), the runs of Team A and Team B.
Output:
- if a > b print: Team A wins by X runs
- if b > a print: Team B wins by X runs
- if they are equal print: Match tied
where X is the difference in runs (always write the word runs, even for 1).

Example: input 180 165 prints Team A wins by 15 runs.
starterCode:
a, b = map(int, input().split())
# your code here

examples.explanation: Both scores are equal.

hints: Use if / elif / else for the three cases.
The margin is the bigger score minus the smaller one.
explanation: Compare the two scores with if, elif and else. In each winning branch print the margin as the larger score minus the smaller; if neither is larger, the match is tied.

title: Train Ticket Fare by Age
statement:
Indian Railways charges a full fare to most passengers. Children below 5 years travel free, and senior citizens aged 60 or more pay half the fare (rounded down, fare // 2).

Input: one line with two integers fare and age (1 <= fare <= 5000, 0 <= age <= 120).
Output: one integer, the fare the passenger pays.

Example: input 840 65 prints 420 because a 65-year-old pays half.
starterCode:
fare, age = map(int, input().split())
# your code here

examples.explanation: Age 65 is a senior citizen, so 840 // 2 = 420.
Children below 5 travel free.

hints: There are three groups: below 5, 60 and above, and everyone else.
Be careful with the boundaries: age 5 pays full fare, age 60 pays half.
explanation: Check the age against the two boundaries with if / elif / else. Print 0 for children under 5, fare // 2 for age 60 and above, and the full fare otherwise.

title: Sum of Train Number Digits
statement:
Ravi likes adding up the digits of train numbers while he waits on the platform.

Input: one integer n (1 <= n <= 10^9), the train number.
Output: one integer, the sum of its digits.

Example: for 12627 the answer is 1 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 7 = 18.
starterCode:
n = int(input())
# your code here
referenceSolution:
n = int(input())
total = 0
while n > 0:
    total += n % 10
    n //= 10
print(total)
hints: n % 10 gives the last digit.
n // 10 removes the last digit; repeat while n > 0.
explanation: Repeatedly take the last digit with n % 10, add it to a running total, and drop it with n // 10. Stop when n becomes 0 and print the total.

title: Multiplication Table
statement:
Print the multiplication table of a number from 1 to 10.

Input: one integer n (1 <= n <= 100).
Output: 10 lines. Line i (i from 1 to 10) is: n x i = p, where p is n * i, with single spaces exactly as shown.

Example: for 3 the first line is 3 x 1 = 3 and the last line is 3 x 10 = 30.
starterCode:
n = int(input())
# your code here

examples.explanation: Each line multiplies 3 by the next number from 1 to 10.

hints: Use for i in range(1, 11).
print(n, "x", i, "=", n * i) puts single spaces between the parts.
explanation: Loop i from 1 to 10 with range(1, 11) and print one formatted line per step containing n, i and their product.

title: Reverse a Number
statement:
Reverse the digits of a number. Leading zeros of the reversed number are dropped, so 1200 becomes 21.

Input: one integer n (0 <= n <= 10^9).
Output: the reversed number as an integer.

Example: 12345 becomes 54321.
starterCode:
n = int(input())
# your code here

examples.explanation: The digits are read from the back.
Reversed it is 0021, and the leading zeros are dropped.

referenceSolution:
n = int(input())
rev = 0
while n > 0:
    rev = rev * 10 + n % 10
    n //= 10
print(rev)
hints: Build the answer digit by digit: rev = rev * 10 + last digit.
Remember that the input can be 0.
explanation: Start with rev = 0. While n is positive, append the last digit of n to rev using rev * 10 + n % 10 and remove it from n with n // 10. Leading zeros vanish automatically because rev is an integer.

title: Piggy Bank Target
statement:
Meena saves Rs 1 on day 1, Rs 2 on day 2, Rs 3 on day 3, and so on. How many days does she need until her total savings reach at least the target?

Input: one integer target (1 <= target <= 10^6).
Output: one integer, the number of days.

Example: for target 10, after 4 days she has 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10, so print 4.
starterCode:
target = int(input())
# your code here

examples.explanation: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 reaches the target on day 4.
After 4 days she has 10, which is short; day 5 brings 15.

referenceSolution:
target = int(input())
total = 0
day = 0
while total < target:
    day += 1
    total += day
print(day)
hints: Keep two variables: the current day and the total saved.
Use a while loop that runs as long as the total is below the target.
explanation: Simulate day by day with a while loop: increase the day counter, add that many rupees to the total, and stop as soon as the total reaches the target. The day counter is the answer.

title: Number Triangle
statement:
Print a triangle of numbers with n rows. Row i contains the numbers 1 to i separated by single spaces.

Input: one integer n (1 <= n <= 20).
Output: n lines as described (no trailing spaces).

Example: for n = 3 print
1
1 2
1 2 3
starterCode:
n = int(input())
# your code here

examples.explanation: Row 1 has 1, row 2 has 1 2, row 3 has 1 2 3.

hints: Use an outer loop for rows and an inner loop for the numbers in a row.
Collect a row as strings and join with spaces to avoid trailing spaces.
explanation: The outer loop runs i from 1 to n, one row each. The inner loop builds the numbers 1 to i, which are joined with single spaces and printed. Nesting loops like this is the basis of every pattern problem.

title: Count the Vowels
statement:
Count how many vowels (a, e, i, o, u, upper or lower case) appear in a line of text.

Input: one line containing letters and spaces only (length 1 to 1000).
Output: one integer, the number of vowels.

Example: Virat Kohli has i, a, o, i, so print 4.
starterCode:
text = input()
# your code here

examples.explanation: The vowels are i, a, o and i.

hints: Convert the text to lower case first so you only check five letters.
ch in "aeiou" tells you whether ch is a vowel.
explanation: Lower-case the line, loop over each character, and increase a counter whenever the character is one of a, e, i, o, u. Spaces and consonants are simply skipped.

title: Palindrome Name
statement:
A word is a palindrome if it reads the same forwards and backwards, ignoring upper and lower case.

Input: one word of letters only (length 1 to 100).
Output: print Yes if it is a palindrome, otherwise No.

Example: Malayalam read backwards is malayalaM, which matches ignoring case, so print Yes.
starterCode:
word = input()
# your code here

examples.explanation: Ignoring case it reads the same both ways.
Backwards it is alarek.

hints: word[::-1] gives the word reversed.
Use .lower() before comparing.
explanation: Lower-case the word and compare it with its reverse, word[::-1]. If they are equal print Yes, otherwise No.

title: Initials of a Name
statement:
Print the initials of a full name in capital letters, separated by dots.

Input: one line with a name made of one or more words separated by single spaces (letters only, total length 1 to 100).
Output: the first letter of each word in upper case, joined with a dot. There is no dot at the end.

Example: sachin ramesh tendulkar prints S.R.T
starterCode:
name = input()
# your code here

examples.explanation: The words start with s, r and t.
A single word gives a single initial with no dot.

referenceSolution:
words = input().split()
letters = []
for w in words:
    letters.append(w[0].upper())
print(".".join(letters))
hints: split() turns the line into a list of words.
".".join(list) puts dots only between items.
explanation: Split the name into words, take the first character of each word in upper case, and join those letters with dots. join adds dots only between items, so there is no trailing dot.

title: Letters, Digits and Symbols
statement:
Classify the characters of a PNR-style code.

Input: one line with no spaces (length 1 to 200) made of letters, digits and symbols.
Output: three integers separated by single spaces: the number of letters, the number of digits, and the number of other characters.

Example: Pnr@2024 has 3 letters (P, n, r), 4 digits and 1 other character (@), so print 3 4 1.
starterCode:
code = input()
# your code here

examples.explanation: P, n, r are letters; 2, 0, 2, 4 are digits; @ is other.

hints: ch.isalpha() and ch.isdigit() test a single character.
Anything that is neither a letter nor a digit counts as other.
explanation: Keep three counters. Loop over the characters and use isalpha, then isdigit, then else to decide which counter to increase. Print the three counters on one line.

title: Compress the String
statement:
Shorten a string by writing each run of the same letter as the letter followed by the run length.

Input: one line of lowercase letters (length 1 to 1000).
Output: the compressed string: for every group of consecutive equal letters, print the letter then its count (even when the count is 1).

Example: aaabcc becomes a3b1c2.
starterCode:
s = input()
# your code here

examples.explanation: aaa, b and cc are the groups.
No letter repeats next to itself, so every group has length 1.

hints: Keep a counter for the current group and compare each letter with the previous one.
Do not forget to add the last group after the loop ends.
explanation: Scan the string comparing each letter with the one before it. While they match, increase the count; when they differ (or the string ends), append the previous letter and its count to the result and reset the count to 1.

title: Secret Message Shift
statement:
Encode a message by shifting every letter k places forward in the alphabet, wrapping from z back to a. Spaces stay as they are.

Input: line 1 has k (0 <= k <= 25). Line 2 has the message: lowercase letters and spaces (length 1 to 1000).
Output: the encoded message.

Example: with k = 3, chai time becomes fkdl wlph (c->f, h->k, a->d, i->l).
starterCode:
k = int(input())
msg = input()
# your code here

examples.explanation: Each letter moves 3 places forward.
y and z wrap around to a and b.

hints: ord(ch) - ord('a') gives the position 0 to 25 of a letter.
Add k, take % 26 to wrap, then turn it back with chr(... + ord('a')).
explanation: For every letter compute its position 0 to 25, add k, wrap with % 26 and convert back to a letter. Spaces are copied unchanged. Building the result character by character keeps the message's layout.

title: Top Score and Its Match
statement:
A batter's scores in n matches are given. Find the highest score and the match number (1-based) where it first happened.

Input: line 1 has n (1 <= n <= 100). Line 2 has n integers (0 <= score <= 300) separated by spaces.
Output: two integers separated by a space: the highest score and the first match number where it was scored.

Example: for scores 34 78 12 78 5 the highest is 78, first scored in match 2, so print 78 2.
starterCode:
n = int(input())
scores = list(map(int, input().split()))
# your code here

examples.explanation: 78 appears in matches 2 and 4; the first is 2.

referenceSolution:
n = int(input())
scores = list(map(int, input().split()))
best = scores[0]
pos = 1
for i in range(1, n):
    if scores[i] > best:
        best = scores[i]
        pos = i + 1
print(best, pos)
hints: Start with the first score as the best so far.
Use > (not >=) so the first occurrence is kept.
explanation: Walk through the list keeping the best score and its position. Update only when a strictly bigger score appears, so ties keep the earlier match. Positions are 1-based, so store i + 1.

title: Fifties and Hundreds
statement:
Count a batter's half-centuries and centuries. A score from 50 to 99 is a fifty; a score of 100 or more is a hundred.

Input: line 1 has n (1 <= n <= 100). Line 2 has n integers (0 <= score <= 300).
Output: two integers separated by a space: the number of fifties and the number of hundreds.

Example: for 45 50 120 99 100 7 there are two fifties (50, 99) and two hundreds (120, 100), so print 2 2.
starterCode:
n = int(input())
scores = list(map(int, input().split()))
# your code here

examples.explanation: 50 and 99 are fifties; 120 and 100 are hundreds.

hints: Check the 100 case first, then the 50 case.
A score of 120 must not be counted as a fifty too.
explanation: Loop over the scores with two counters. Test s >= 100 first so centuries are not also counted as fifties, then use elif s >= 50 for the fifties.

title: Sum of Even Numbers
statement:
Add up only the even numbers in a list.

Input: line 1 has n (1 <= n <= 100). Line 2 has n integers (-1000 <= x <= 1000).
Output: one integer, the sum of the even numbers (print 0 if there are none).

Example: for 3 8 -4 7 10 the even numbers are 8, -4 and 10, so print 14.
starterCode:
n = int(input())
nums = list(map(int, input().split()))
# your code here
referenceSolution:
n = int(input())
nums = list(map(int, input().split()))
total = 0
for x in nums:
    if x % 2 == 0:
        total += x
print(total)
hints: x % 2 == 0 means x is even, and it also works for negative numbers in Python.
Start the sum at 0 so a list with no even numbers prints 0.
explanation: Start a total at 0, loop through the numbers and add those whose remainder on division by 2 is 0. Print the total.

title: Longest Rising Streak
statement:
A batter's runs in consecutive innings are given. Find the length of the longest run of innings where every score is strictly higher than the one before it.

Input: line 1 has n (1 <= n <= 1000). Line 2 has n integers (0 <= runs <= 300).
Output: one integer, the length of the longest strictly increasing streak of consecutive innings (a single innings counts as 1).

Example: for 10 20 15 25 30 40 the longest streak is 15 25 30 40, so print 4.
starterCode:
n = int(input())
runs = list(map(int, input().split()))
# your code here

examples.explanation: 15, 25, 30, 40 rise each time.

hints: Keep the length of the current streak and the best length seen.
Equal scores break the streak because it must be strictly higher.
explanation: Walk through the list comparing each score with the previous one. If it is higher, extend the current streak; otherwise restart it at 1. Track the largest streak seen and print it.

title: Pairs That Make the Bill
statement:
Two friends want to spend exactly a target amount by buying two different items. Count how many pairs of items (i, j) with i < j have prices adding up to the target.

Input: line 1 has n (1 <= n <= 200). Line 2 has n integers (-1000 <= price <= 1000). Line 3 has the target (-2000 <= target <= 2000).
Output: one integer, the number of pairs.

Example: for 1 5 7 -1 5 and target 6 the pairs are (1, 5), (1, 5) and (7, -1), so print 3.
starterCode:
n = int(input())
prices = list(map(int, input().split()))
target = int(input())
# your code here

examples.explanation: 1 pairs with each 5, and 7 pairs with -1.

hints: Use two nested loops: j starts at i + 1 so each pair is counted once.
With a single item there are no pairs.
explanation: Check every pair with two nested loops where the inner index starts after the outer one, so no pair is counted twice and no item pairs with itself. Count the pairs whose sum equals the target.

Write a function is_prime(n) that returns True when n is prime, and use it to check one number. A prime has exactly two divisors, 1 and itself; 1 is not prime.

Input: one integer n (1 <= n <= 10^6).
Output: print Prime or Not Prime.

Example: 97 has no divisor between 2 and 9 (since 10 * 10 > 97), so print Prime.

title: Price with GST
statement:
Write a function with_gst(price, rate) that returns the price after adding GST at rate percent, and print the result for one item.

Input: one line with two integers price and rate (1 <= price <= 100000; rate is one of 0, 5, 12, 18, 28).
Output: the final price with exactly 2 digits after the decimal point.

Example: input 199 18 gives 199 + 35.82 = 234.82.
starterCode:
def with_gst(price, rate):
    # your code here
    pass

price, rate = map(int, input().split())

examples.explanation: No GST, still printed with 2 decimals.

referenceSolution:
def with_gst(price, rate):
    return price * (100 + rate)  # total in paise

price, rate = map(int, input().split())
paise = with_gst(price, rate)
print(str(paise // 100) + "." + str(paise % 100).zfill(2))
hints: GST amount = price * rate / 100.
Format with f"{value:.2f}" to always show two decimals.
explanation: The function adds price * rate / 100 to the price. Because price and rate are whole numbers the answer has at most two decimals, so printing it with two decimal places (for example f"{x:.2f}") gives an exact result.

title: Grade Card
statement:
Write a function grade(marks) that returns a letter grade, then print the grades of a class.
Grades: 90 or more is A, 75 to 89 is B, 60 to 74 is C, 40 to 59 is D, below 40 is F.

Input: line 1 has n (1 <= n <= 100). Line 2 has n integers (0 <= marks <= 100).
Output: the n grades on one line separated by single spaces.

Example: marks 95 74 40 39 give A C D F.

title: Unique Library Visitors
statement:
The library register lists the name of every visit, and the same student may visit many times. Count how many different students visited.

Input: line 1 has n (1 <= n <= 1000). Line 2 has n names separated by spaces (each name is one word; names are case-sensitive).
Output: one integer, the number of different names.

Example: Anu Ravi Anu Kiran Ravi has 3 different names.
starterCode:
n = int(input())
names = input().split()
# your code here

examples.explanation: Anu, Ravi and Kiran.

testCases.input:
6
A B C D E F

The answer is the number of keys stored.

title: Most Ordered Snack
statement:
A canteen records each order as one word. Find the snack ordered most often.

Input: one line of lowercase words separated by single spaces (1 to 1000 words).
Output: the most frequent word and its count separated by a space. If several words share the highest count, print the one that appears first in the line.

Example: chai samosa chai vada samosa chai prints chai 3.
starterCode:
orders = input().split()
# your code here

examples.input: chai samosa chai vada samosa chai
examples.explanation: chai appears 3 times, samosa 2, vada 1.
Both appear twice; vada comes first.

testCases.input: chai samosa chai vada samosa chai
x y y x z z z

hints: Count with counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1.
For ties, scan the words in their original order and only switch on a strictly bigger count.
explanation: First build a dictionary of counts. Then scan the words in input order, keeping the best word and replacing it only when a word has a strictly higher count; this makes the earliest word win ties.

title: Anagram Check
statement:
Two words are anagrams if they use exactly the same letters the same number of times, like listen and silent.

Input: two lines, each with one lowercase word (length 1 to 1000).
Output: print Yes if they are anagrams, otherwise No.

Example: listen and silent both have one each of e, i, l, n, s, t, so print Yes.
starterCode:
a = input()
b = input()
# your code here

examples.explanation: Same letters, same counts.
a appears twice in the first word but once in the second.

Two dictionaries can be compared directly with ==.
explanation: Build a letter-count dictionary for each word and compare them with ==. Words of different lengths or with any letter count mismatch give different dictionaries, so the answer is No.

title: Canteen Order Total
statement:
The canteen menu lists each item with its price. Given the orders of the day, compute the total bill.

Input: line 1 has m (1 <= m <= 50), the number of menu items. The next m lines each have an item name (one word) and its price (1 to 500). Then a line with k (1 <= k <= 100), the number of orders. The next k lines each have an item name and a quantity (1 to 20). Every ordered item is on the menu.
Output: one integer, the total amount.

Example: menu tea 10, samosa 15; orders tea 2, samosa 3, tea 1 give 30 + 45 = 75.
starterCode:
m = int(input())
# read the m menu lines, then the orders

examples.explanation: tea: 3 x 10 = 30, samosa: 3 x 15 = 45.

testCases.input:
2
thali 500
puri 40
4
thali 20
puri 1
puri 1
thali 1

referenceSolution:
m = int(input())
price = {}
for _ in range(m):
    name, p = input().split()
    price[name] = int(p)
k = int(input())
total = 0
for _ in range(k):
    name, qty = input().split()
    total += price[name] * int(qty)
print(total)
hints: Store the menu in a dictionary from item name to price.
For every order, look up the price and multiply by the quantity.
explanation: Read the menu into a dictionary so each price can be found instantly by name. Then read each order, multiply the looked-up price by the quantity and add it to the total.

title: Top Three Scores
statement:
Print the three highest scores of a tournament, highest first. Equal scores are listed separately.

Input: line 1 has n (3 <= n <= 100). Line 2 has n integers (0 <= score <= 1000).
Output: the three highest scores in descending order, separated by single spaces.

Example: for 45 89 12 89 70 print 89 89 70.
starterCode:
n = int(input())
scores = list(map(int, input().split()))
# your code here

examples.explanation: Sorted high to low: 89 89 70 45 12.

referenceSolution:
n = int(input())
scores = list(map(int, input().split()))
scores.sort(reverse=True)
print(scores[0], scores[1], scores[2])
hints: list.sort(reverse=True) sorts from high to low.
After sorting, the first three items are the answer.
explanation: Sort the scores in descending order and print the first three. Duplicates stay in the list, so equal top scores are both printed.

title: Class Rank List
statement:
Print the students in rank order: higher marks first; students with equal marks are listed in alphabetical order of name.

Input: line 1 has n (1 <= n <= 100). The next n lines each have a name (one word, unique) and marks (0 to 100).
Output: n lines, one name per line, in rank order.

Example: Ravi 85, Anu 92, Kiran 85 gives Anu, then Kiran, then Ravi (Kiran comes before Ravi alphabetically).
starterCode:
n = int(input())
# read the n lines of name and marks

examples.explanation: Anu has the most marks; Kiran and Ravi tie and go alphabetically.

referenceSolution:
n = int(input())
students = []
for _ in range(n):
    name, marks = input().split()
    students.append((-int(marks), name))
students.sort()
for m, name in students:
    print(name)
hints: Store each student as a tuple and sort the list.
Using (-marks, name) makes sort put higher marks first and break ties by name.
explanation: Store each student as the tuple (-marks, name). Sorting tuples compares the first item and then the second, so negated marks give descending marks and names break ties alphabetically. Print the names in sorted order.

title: Closest Train Arrivals
statement:
Arrival times of trains at a station are given in minutes after midnight, in no particular order. Find the smallest gap in minutes between any two arrivals.

Input: line 1 has n (2 <= n <= 1000). Line 2 has n integers (0 <= time <= 1439).
Output: one integer, the smallest difference between any two arrival times (0 if two trains arrive at the same minute).

Example: for 600 545 720 610 the sorted times are 545 600 610 720; the gaps are 55, 10 and 110, so print 10.
starterCode:
n = int(input())
times = list(map(int, input().split()))
# your code here

examples.explanation: After sorting, 600 and 610 are the closest neighbours.

referenceSolution:
n = int(input())
times = list(map(int, input().split()))
times.sort()
best = times[1] - times[0]
for i in range(2, n):
    if times[i] - times[i - 1] < best:
        best = times[i] - times[i - 1]
print(best)
hints: After sorting, the closest pair is always next to each other.
Compare only neighbouring times instead of every pair.
explanation: Sort the times; the smallest gap must then be between two neighbours, so one pass over adjacent pairs finds it. This is faster and simpler than comparing every pair with nested loops.
